incentives.question: Is the PTC still relevant in 2026, after the One Big Beautiful Bill Act?
incentives.answer: Yes, for nuclear specifically. The OBBBA (signed July 2025) terminated the tech-neutral §45Y/§48E credits early for wind and solar but kept them for nuclear: a nuclear plant qualifies if construction begins before 2034, with a three-year phase-out after that. The deployments this site tracks target operation between 2028 and 2030, comfortably inside that window; most rows publish no construction date, so start-of-construction timing is an open item per project.

points.fact: §45Y/§48E survive for new nuclear that begins construction before 2034, then phase out over three years; the emissions-based sunset trigger was replaced by these fixed dates.

reading:
What matters is where the bands overlap. Against **rural Alaska** — which the state regulator puts at **$410–1,950/MWh**, and where commercial customers get no PCE subsidy — even a **first-of-a-kind** microreactor at $140–410 wins across the whole range. That is the one market where the cost case is not in doubt, and it is why Fort Wainwright is the row worth watching in the Army Janus table.

Against **remote industrial diesel** at $250–600 the bands cross. A first unit at the top of its range loses to cheap diesel at the bottom of its. So 'cheaper than diesel' is a claim you have to make site by site, and it turns on how hard the fuel is to deliver, until **later units** at $90–330 arrive.

Against ordinary grid power in the U.S., the microreactor loses in every published case except one that assumes the tax credit ($48–78), which is a forecast rather than a price anyone has paid. The upshot is that the sales pitch changes by sector. Off-grid sites can buy on cost right now. On-grid sites are buying resilience, speed, or clean power, and paying extra for it.

capex.note: Everything above is a price per unit of energy. This is the price per unit of capacity, which is what a buyer actually signs for. capex.reading: The gap between $22,000/kWe and $2,515/kWe is the whole argument about microreactors. Nobody has built enough of them to say which end is right. Any figure quoted without saying which unit it describes — the first or the hundredth — is not telling you anything.

learning_curve.question: What does the 20th unit cost, and what never gets cheaper?
learning_curve.formula: cost of unit N = cost of unit 1 x (1 - learning rate) ^ log2(N)
learning_curve.worked: INL runs this at a learning rate of 8% over 20 units. That works out to a multiplier of about 0.70 — the 20th unit costs roughly 30% less than the first. But the multiplier is only applied to work done at the site. Other parts of the bill fall much faster, and some do not fall at all.

classes.detail: Reactor vessel and internals, control drums, shielding, pumps, heat exchangers, instrumentation, and fabricating the first core's fuel assemblies. A 70% cut, taken from a study of a dedicated line building 10 units a year.

classes.klass: Falls slowly — work done at the site
classes.detail: Site preparation, buildings, startup, shipping, engineering, project and construction management, licensing and regulatory cost. This is the 8%-over-20-units curve.
Land, permits, plant studies, the initial coolant, mining, converting and enriching the first core, recruiting and training operators, technicians and security, refueling, and spent fuel management.

learning_curve.floor: The third row is the one that decides whether this technology works. Uranium, and the people who run and guard the plant, cost the same on the 20th unit as on the first. INL models 6 to 10 full-time staff at $162,000 to $188,000 each. That is the floor the curve flattens onto, and it is why the levelized cost stops falling well above zero.
learning_curve.rates: Where INL does apply a rate, it varies by component: 8% for work at the site, 18% for the reactor's primary structure, 23% for plant equipment and instrumentation, 24% for the reactivity control system, and 40% for anything made of beryllium.
learning_curve.definitions_warning: The two INL reports do not mean the same thing by "Nth-of-a-kind". The 2024 report computes learning over 20 units. The 2025 report assumes cost stops falling after 100. Numbers from the two are not interchangeable.

archetypes.question: Does the choice of reactor type change the answer?
archetypes.note: INL costed three generic designs with the same tool, so they can be compared directly. These are the lab's own reference designs, not any company's product. No vendor's reactor is priced here.

rows.analogue: INL's own reference design. No announced military microreactor uses it.
The closest published archetype to the gas-cooled designs in the field, including Radiant's Kaleidos, BWXT's BANR and General Atomics' GA-TES.
The closest published archetype to the heat-pipe designs, including Antares' R1 and Westinghouse's eVinci.

archetypes.finding: The heat-pipe archetype is by far the most expensive in INL's model, at $980/MWh for a first unit against $330 for the liquid-metal design. Most of that gap is size, not technology: the heat-pipe case is modeled at 7 MWt against 20 MWt, and INL's own sensitivity says halving a reactor's output raises its levelized cost by about half. The rest is fuel — INL cites work putting heat-pipe fuel cost at two to three times other microreactor types, and its major equipment at about twice. The modeled unit also refuels every 3 years, where Antares states 6 or more for the R1.
archetypes.convergence: Type matters far more for the first unit than the twentieth. The liquid-metal design is 25% cheaper than the gas-cooled one as a first unit, but only 6% cheaper once both are mass-produced.
